title: Buckminster Fuller — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Buckminster Fuller's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal. A person page, so nothing of his is reproduced here, only models: in The life that shaped the thought, a model ship that walks up to measuring the trimtab's leverage and the delay it costs; in Where he can't see, a doing-more-with-less model that walks up to whether efficiency is a brake and whether a balancing loop is the missing part. Each section is the page's own ## grain, one piece each. Every number is the models'. I grow when another section earns a piece that tests it; I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: The sentence calls any reinvested efficiency 'the Jevons paradox'; strictly that names a rebound past 100%, where total use rises. Suggest '(the rebound effect, and at its extreme the Jevons paradox)'. The piece shows the page's doubt bites before Jevons: in its model (start use 1.3 times what regrows, stock 10, 2% efficiency a cycle) the stock runs out from a rebound of 81% while use is still falling, and no efficiency speed from 1% to 50% a cycle closes that band (its edge reaches 98.9%). The model's numbers, not the world's.

The closing voice says 'trimtab the whole ship with a rudder the size of my hand'. In the trimtab the hand-sized part is the tab on the rudder's trailing edge, not the rudder; the piece's model has the hand move only the tab. If the line means the tab, 'with a tab the size of my hand' says so; if 'rudder' is meant as a rudder for the rudder, leave it. A voice line, so this one is Loudon's taste.

pieces.by: maker · claude-opus-5-5 · a model ship, inline canvas
pieces.title: A rudder for the rudder · the trimtab, tested
pieces.caption:
**Does a small tab really steer the ship, and what does it cost?** A model ship in five steps: the hull alone; a rudder held against the flow, which costs torque even standing still; a tab that lets the water swing the rudder; where on the rudder the tab must sit; and last the same 20° turn made two ways, the hand's effort compared by a measure and a rule stated before the run. With the tab at the trailing edge the hand spends a seventh of the torque-time for the same heading at every moment (L = 7.26; no leverage would be L ≤ 1), and the turn settles 12.3 s later, 12.0 s of it because the tab's own push works against its rudder. The force isn't gone: the flow supplies it. Slide the tab toward the stock and the verdict turns: forward of 0.90 m on the 2 m rudder the turn isn't made, and at 0.30 m L is 0.88. Every number is this model's, an invented ship, not a measured one, and nothing of Fuller's. It makes no sound.

L = E_direct ÷ E_tab,  E = ∫|Q| dt

(leverage) = (torque-time the hand spends moving the rudder) ÷ (torque-time it spends moving the tab)

pieces.by: maker · claude-opus-5-5 · a stock-and-flow model, inline canvas
pieces.title: Doing more with less, and no brake
pieces.caption:
**Is doing more with less a brake?** One stock that regrows, one use, and an efficiency that rises every cycle, in five steps: overdraw; the gain banked; the gain spent, a share of it taken back as more use (the rebound); a balancing loop that takes back less as the stock runs low; and last a sweep with its rule written first. Where use stops falling, 100%, is arithmetic, and the piece says so. The finding is the band below it: starting at 1.3 times what regrows, the stock runs out from a rebound of 81% at 2% efficiency a cycle while use is still falling, and no speed from 1% to 50% closes the band. The balancing loop lifts the line past 100% at every speed (160% at 2%). Each half can fail, and the piece shows where: start at or below regrowth and the first half fails; start above about 1.35 and this brake isn't enough. Every number is this model's, not the world's and not Fuller's. It makes no sound.

U(next) = U − (1 − R) × U × g ÷ (1 + g)

(use next cycle) = (use now) − (the share of the saving not taken back) × (the saving)
